lessons.title: Inflation and changing plans
lessons.goal: Explain how a changing price level can alter purchasing power, compare nominal amounts with real purchasing power, and use scenarios to keep a financial plan adaptable.
lessons.opening: Your fictional savings balance rises from $100 to $101. During the same year, the basket of items you planned to buy rises from $100 to $103. Did your money grow? The balance is larger, but the question is whether it can still buy as much.
teach: Inflation describes a general rise in prices across a basket of goods and services over time. It does not mean every price rises by the same amount: a particular item may become cheaper, rise sharply, or stay similar while the overall basket changes. A published inflation measure is a summary for a defined place, time, and basket. It is useful evidence, not a forecast of one household's exact costs. For this lesson, the $100 basket and its later price are invented teaching numbers. They are not a Canadian Consumer Price Index result and should never be quoted as one.

Keep nominal dollars and purchasing power separate. A nominal balance is the number displayed in an account. Purchasing power asks what that balance can buy at the relevant prices. If an account balance moves from $100 to $101 while a comparable fictional basket moves from $100 to $103, the balance is nominally up one dollar but the basket now costs more. The ratio $101 ÷ $103 ≈ 0.9806 means the later balance buys about 98.06% of the original basket in this simplified comparison. This is a comparison of the stated basket only; it does not measure a person's full life or prove a particular account is unsuitable.

For a plan, inflation is one uncertainty among income, timing, fees, access, and changing goals. Make a useful scenario instead of pretending to know the future: state a current cost, choose a clearly labelled hypothetical price change, calculate the changed target, then ask whether the contribution or timeline still works. Avoid applying an annual percentage repeatedly without explaining compounding and the period. If you consult an official inflation series, record its geography, dates, basket definition, and publication date. Do not use one recent statistic as a guaranteed future rate or treat a broad index as a personal cost-of-living calculator.

A resilient response can combine options: increase a contribution only if the budget can support it, extend the timeline, choose a different version of the goal, reduce another cost, or seek current qualified guidance. Each option has a trade-off. A young person should not be told that market investing is the answer to a short-term price change; value can fall precisely when cash is needed. Keep near-term needs and emergency access in view, and compare long-term choices using fees, risk, and time horizon. The FINLIT Investing Money video introduces purchasing power; use only its conceptual segment and stop before its dated generalization about a usual inflation target. The essential learning remains in this explanation and the calculation below.

lessons.title: Review a complete financial plan
lessons.goal: Assemble a realistic fictional financial plan by matching goals, time horizons, cash access, accounts and products, costs, uncertainty, and available support.
lessons.opening: A fictional learner has two goals: replace a laptop before the next school year and save toward training after graduation. A single account or investment choice may not suit both timelines. Your job is to make the plan coherent, not to pick a “best” product in the abstract.
teach: A financial plan is a connected set of decisions: what matters, when money is needed, what resources are available, what may change, and how the learner will review the plan. Begin with a goal stated in observable terms. “Be financially successful” is too broad to check; “set aside a fictional amount for a training deposit by a stated month” has a target and a time horizon. Goals may conflict. A near-term need can compete with a longer-term goal for the same dollars, so a plan should name the trade-off rather than pretend every goal can be funded at once.

Next, distinguish an account from a financial product held in or associated with it. An account is an arrangement for holding or accessing money; a product is an asset or service with features, costs, risk, and terms. The words are not interchangeable. A savings account can provide accessible funds, subject to its terms; an investment can rise or fall and may be unsuitable for a near-term purchase. The name of an account alone does not establish eligibility, tax treatment, protection, fees, or suitability. Verify the current terms with an official provider or qualified source before a real decision.

Match each goal to its time horizon and consequences if the value is lower or money is temporarily unavailable. Ask: when is it needed, how certain is the date, what minimum amount is required, what access restrictions or withdrawal costs apply, and can the learner tolerate a loss? A plan can use separate “buckets” for clarity without implying separate real accounts. Keep a contingency for unexpected costs if the scenario permits. Do not use a high projected return to make an infeasible contribution schedule appear workable. Contributions should be checked against fictional income and essential expenses, with the remaining amount visible.

A complete plan also tracks assumptions and revision triggers. State whether a return is illustrative, whether fees or inflation are included, and what evidence will be checked again. FINLIT’s planning material usefully prompts learners to connect goals, time, savings, and investments; this course rebuilds those prompts into an original evidence-based plan, omitting dated benefit amounts, historic rates, and unsupported guarantees. The selected video excerpt makes the teaching point that planning still has value when some variables are unknown. Unknowns are a reason to document assumptions and test scenarios, not a reason to claim certainty or give up.

Finally, identify when another person or institution should help. A trusted adult or teacher may help a student understand a decision; a financial institution can explain its own product terms; a regulated or qualified professional may be appropriate for complex personal advice. The student should know what question to ask and how to verify the source. Do not request real household balances, account statements, passwords, SINs, or credit reports for a class assignment. The fictional worksheet below intentionally includes enough figures to test whether the plan balances while leaving personal information out.

lessons.title: Test a plan against change
lessons.goal: Use transparent scenarios to test a fictional financial plan, distinguish uncertainty from prediction, and revise one decision when a cost, contribution, or investment value changes.
lessons.opening: A plan looks balanced until an unexpected $80 expense appears. Another version shows a market value falling just before money is needed. A strong plan does not hide either case: it shows what changes, which assumptions matter, and what response is feasible.
teach: A scenario test asks, “If this specified change occurs, what happens to the plan?” It is not a prediction. Name the baseline, alter one or two variables, recalculate, and explain the consequence. This isolates cause and effect. For example, use fictional market value $500 and compare three one-year outcomes: a 15% loss, no change, or a 6% increase. Applying those percentages gives $425, $500, and $530 before any fees, tax, inflation, contributions, or product rules. These are simple arithmetic illustrations, not expected outcomes or financial advice.

The lesson’s simulator separates time horizon from uncertainty. Money required soon may have little time to recover from a decline; money intended for a distant goal can still lose value, and a longer timeline does not eliminate risk. A scenario is useful when it exposes consequences the student can tolerate or cannot tolerate. Never present the positive case as the normal result or the loss case as impossible. If a product has fees or withdrawals, those terms would need to be added from current verified documentation. Keep the basic calculator transparent so every student can reproduce it without trusting a black box.

Test cash flow too. Suppose a fictional learner begins with $200 for a goal and plans to contribute $25 per month for six months. The simple no-growth total is $350. If an $80 unexpected expense is paid from that same goal fund in month two, the remaining amount becomes $120 at that point. Six further deposits of $30 would add $180, producing $300, still below the original $350 target. The plan must change: amount, timeline, target, or another funding source. State which resource is actually available; do not count the same dollars for two goals.

A useful revision has a reason and a check date. If a short-term goal is underfunded, extending the date may be safer than taking more risk, but circumstances vary. If the need is essential and immediate, the student should seek a trusted adult or appropriate support instead of treating a classroom simulation as personal advice. The FINLIT compounding lesson can help students visualize how time and reinvested gains interact, but its later numerical examples must not be used as guaranteed growth or copied uncritically. This lesson uses the conceptual “snowball” segment only, then contrasts it with negative, flat, and positive scenarios.

When reviewing a result, ask four questions: (1) What changed? (2) Which total or risk changed because of it? (3) What is the consequence if the original target date stays fixed? (4) What revision best fits the stated priorities? A strong response can say what remains unknown. It should also name the simplifications: no fees, taxes, inflation, contributions, or product-specific rules unless the scenario explicitly includes them. This habit makes a student’s reasoning inspectable and transferable to future information without claiming to forecast markets.

lessons.title: Digital footprints and financial security
lessons.goal: Identify how digital traces and account habits can increase or reduce financial-information exposure, and select practical security steps without disclosing personal information.
lessons.opening: A fictional learner posts a photo showing a team hoodie, a bus stop sign, and the time they leave home. In a different app, they reuse a password and receive an unexpected sign-in code. None of these clues alone proves account compromise, but together they create avoidable exposure.
teach: A digital footprint is the trail of information created when people post, search, message, sign in, or use connected devices. Some information is deliberately shared; other information can be inferred from images, timing, location tags, public profiles, data brokers, or old accounts. A footprint is not a moral score and students should not be asked to reveal or defend their own posts. We use a fictional profile to practise asking: what can a stranger learn, what might be reused elsewhere, and what could a person change? A detail that seems harmless alone may become identifying when combined with other details.

Protect account access with unique passwords or passphrases for important accounts, a reputable password manager where appropriate, and multi-factor authentication when available. Never share a one-time verification code, password, recovery phrase, or remote-access control with someone who unexpectedly contacts you. A legitimate service may use verification steps, but you should initiate contact through a trusted route if uncertain. A code arriving unexpectedly can mean someone mistyped a number or is attempting sign-in; do not approve it just to stop the messages. Use account security settings to review active sessions, recovery details, and alerts.

Reduce what is exposed: make profile audiences intentional, avoid posting real-time location or predictable routines, remove unnecessary app permissions, update devices and apps, use a screen lock, and use secure networks for sensitive work. These are layers, not guarantees. Public Wi-Fi does not automatically mean every transaction is unsafe, and a padlock icon does not prove a website or offer is honest. Check the domain and reach a service independently. If someone else’s image or data is involved, get permission before sharing and consider whether reposting could expose them.

For a practical audit, label each fictional detail as public, limited, or private; then identify one plausible misuse and one proportionate control. Prioritize credentials and recovery routes because one reused password may unlock more than one account. If an account may already be accessed, secure it from a trusted device using the independently located service, change the exposed password and any reused password, end unknown sessions if possible, and contact the provider. The order can vary with account type and urgency, so use the provider’s current official instructions.

FINLIT’s Avoiding Scams video gives a short reminder that personal information and passwords deserve protection. This course adds the reasoning and practice: students inspect a made-up profile, minimize exposure, and rehearse how not to share a code. No real passwords, usernames, account screenshots, phone numbers, location histories, or private family details belong in this assignment. When the scenario requires personal reflection, use a fictional persona instead.

lessons.title: Recognize scams and verify independently
lessons.goal: Identify pressure, unusual payment or information requests, suspicious links, and impersonation cues; explain why appearance alone is not proof and verify through an independently located channel.
lessons.opening: Two messages arrive on the same day. One claims that a bank transfer is “at risk” and demands a code through a link. Another says a tax account has a new notice and directs the recipient to sign in through Canada.ca. Which is suspicious? Which might be legitimate? The answer requires checking the request and route, not guessing from tone or logo.
teach: A scam is an attempt to deceive someone for money, access, or information. Common indicators include urgency, secrecy, threats, an unexpected prize or refund, requests to move money, requests for passwords or one-time codes, remote access demands, unusual payment methods, and links that do not match the organization’s independently located address. Grammar and logos are weak tests: a polished message can be fraudulent, and a legitimate notice can look plain. One indicator raises a question; it does not by itself prove who sent the message.

Use a verification routine: pause; do not click, reply, transfer money, or share a code while pressured; identify what action is requested; locate the organization’s contact route independently using a trusted official website, app, card, statement, or known number; and ask whether the request is genuine. Do not use the phone number, link, or caller ID supplied by the suspicious contact. Search results and ads can also be misleading, so navigate to the known official domain and inspect it carefully. If in doubt, tell a trusted person and ask for help without forwarding sensitive information.

Government and financial contacts require nuance. The Canada Revenue Agency can contact people by phone, automated message, letter, and email notifications, depending on the situation. Therefore, the blanket claim “CRA never calls” is false and must not be taught. At the same time, a caller ID can be spoofed and a caller’s claim is not proof. CRA guidance says a person may ask for the caller’s name, office, and callback number, end the call, and independently verify through CRA’s official contact-verification tool or a number found on Canada.ca. A legitimate contact may ask for some information during identity verification or to resolve missing tax information; students should not infer legitimacy solely because a caller knows details. Never share passwords or security codes with an unexpected caller.

For suspicious email or text, avoid opening attachments or links; inspect the request without interacting, then independently access the account or contact channel. If the message asks for an immediate “safe account” transfer, gift cards, crypto, e-transfer, a remote-access app, or a code, stop and verify. Legitimate institutions may have fraud-prevention procedures, but move only after contacting them through independently sourced details. Do not call a message safe just because it names a real organization; impersonation is the tactic.

This course deliberately crops the video before that statement and replaces it with current CRA guidance. Students classify fictional messages by evidence, state what remains uncertain, and choose a safe verification route. The goal is not to make learners suspicious of every contact; it is to slow an irreversible action until the request and channel are independently checked.

lessons.title: Respond when information may be exposed
lessons.goal: Choose a safe first response when a learner interacts with a suspicious message, protect accounts and payment routes, preserve evidence, and report through appropriate channels without shame or false promises.
lessons.opening: A fictional learner clicks a bank-looking link and enters a password, then realizes the address was wrong. No money has moved yet. The next steps matter, but panic and blame do not help. Work through a response that starts with account protection and uses official contact routes.
teach: If a suspicious link was opened but no information was entered, close it and do not download anything or grant permissions. If a password, code, card number, or identity detail was entered, treat that information as exposed and act promptly. Use a trusted device and independently locate the real service’s app or website; do not return through the message. Change the exposed password and every reused version. If a code or authentication prompt was shared or approved, review sessions and recovery methods, revoke unfamiliar devices when possible, and follow the provider’s current account-recovery process.

If payment details, a card, or money transfer may be involved, contact the financial institution or payment provider immediately using its official number or app found separately. Explain what happened, when, and what information was shared; follow the provider’s instructions for blocking a card, disputing a transaction, or securing an account. Acting quickly can help limit harm, but do not promise that money will always be recovered or that every transaction has identical protections. Keep records of who you contacted and any reference number, without putting secrets into a school submission.

Preserve evidence before deleting the message: save the sender information, screenshots, transaction receipts, web address as text, dates, and provider communications. Do not click again to gather evidence. If money was lost or there is a safety concern, contact local police promptly and ask for a file or incident number. Report suspected fraud or cybercrime to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre (CAFC); its reporting system accepts reports from victims and witnesses, and the centre supports investigations by collecting information. Reporting does not itself guarantee an investigation or repayment.

Tell a trusted adult if you are a minor or feel overwhelmed. There is no benefit in shaming someone for being deceived; scams are designed to pressure people and can look convincing. If identity information or credit may have been exposed, contact affected institutions and consider credit-bureau alerts through current official channels. For tax-related identity concerns, contact CRA using independently verified contact information. Do not report a routine suspicious text as an emergency; use 911 only for immediate danger. Avoid “recovery” services that demand an upfront fee or ask for more access—CAFC warns that fraud victims can be targeted again.

Use a sequence rather than a rigid universal checklist: stop further interaction; identify what was exposed; secure the relevant account/device; contact the payment or service provider; preserve evidence; report to police when money or safety is involved and to CAFC; then monitor and update credentials or identity protections. The exact order may change—for example, a stolen card needs an immediate issuer call. The lesson’s fictional case and the official sources help students choose a proportionate response. No real incident details, account data, or identifying evidence are required for this assignment.

lessons.title: Consumer protection and unfair offers
lessons.goal: Analyze a fictional consumer offer for misleading overall impressions, hidden conditions, and transaction evidence; choose a proportionate Alberta or federal reporting route without promising a refund.
lessons.opening: An online listing advertises a fictional tablet for $120. At checkout, a mandatory “activation fee” adds $80, while a banner still says “all-in price.” The seller says the promotion ends in five minutes. Is this a poor deal, a misleading representation, a scam, or more than one? Work from the claim, transaction, and evidence before choosing a next step.
teach: Consumer protection helps people make informed transactions and gives routes for certain unfair practices. Start by recording the specific representation: the headline, price, feature, availability, refund promise, or condition. Then compare it with the overall impression a reasonable consumer could take away and with the final contract or checkout. A technically true line buried in small print may not undo a prominent false or misleading impression. Pressure tactics, material omissions, bait pricing, and failure to deliver can raise concerns, but a single scenario does not establish a legal violation. Avoid naming conduct unlawful without checking the applicable rule and facts.

For Alberta transactions, the Consumer Protection Act and its rules address unfair practices before, during, and after consumer transactions. Alberta’s consumer guidance gives examples such as misleading claims, pressure, and failing to deliver what was promised. A practical first step for a dispute about a supplier is to contact the business in writing, state the facts and requested resolution, and keep a copy. If unresolved, a consumer may file a complaint with Alberta’s Consumer Investigations Unit (CIU) where appropriate. CIU can investigate potential violations; it does not recover a consumer’s financial loss or mediate a private dispute, and it does not investigate scam texts or calls. Do not imply that submitting a complaint guarantees an outcome.

The Competition Bureau deals with deceptive marketing practices under federal competition law, including materially false or misleading representations; it considers the general impression as well as literal wording. It accepts information about such practices but is not the route for an individual refund. A consumer who paid through a card, marketplace, or financial institution may also need to contact that provider about its own dispute process, using official channels. These paths can overlap, but they have different roles. A scam that impersonates an organization and an unfair seller transaction are not automatically the same category. Determine whether there was a real seller/contract, what was promised, whether the transaction was completed, and whether money or account access is at risk.

Keep a clean evidence record: screenshot the advertisement and checkout, save the terms in effect on the transaction date, keep receipts and delivery messages, note dates and the seller’s contact details, and write down what resolution was requested. Do not post personal payment information publicly. If the seller’s offer may be a scam, avoid sending more money or identity information until independently checked; report fraud through CAFC guidance when appropriate. For a lawful contract, cancellation rights vary by transaction type and current law. Do not tell students that every purchase has a general cooling-off period or refund right. Verify the specific product, transaction method, jurisdiction, and applicable current guidance.

In this course, students identify the exact claim, compare the complete impression with the final amount, distinguish the available reporting routes, and explain what each can and cannot do. All prices and statements in the document are invented. The lesson does not give individualized legal advice or decide a real complaint. Its goal is to help a learner preserve evidence, ask a clear question, and select a competent source rather than relying on a threatening countdown or a social-media opinion.

lessons.title: Recover safely after a scam
lessons.goal: Build a calm, prioritized recovery plan after a fictional scam by matching actions to exposed money, credentials, identity information, or tax details, and avoid secondary recovery fraud.
lessons.opening: A fictional person paid a suspicious invoice and also entered a reused password. They now receive messages promising guaranteed recovery for an upfront fee. Recovery is not one generic form: the right first actions depend on what was exposed, and a second scam can target people who have already lost money.
teach: Begin by separating four kinds of exposure: money/payment route, account credentials, identity or credit information, and tax information. More than one can apply. If money was transferred or a card/payment detail was exposed, promptly contact the financial institution, card issuer, or payment provider through a number or app obtained independently. Ask what immediate security, block, dispute, or recall steps apply and record the time and reference. Do not assume a particular charge will be refunded; institutions review disputes under applicable rules and circumstances. If passwords were exposed, use a trusted device, independently access each affected service, change the password and reused versions, review sessions/recovery details, and enable stronger verification where available.

If identity details or credit information may be misused, contact affected organizations and consider placing fraud alerts with Equifax and TransUnion using their official channels. Check credit reports through current official guidance for unfamiliar accounts or inquiries. Security-freeze availability and procedures can vary by province or territory, so do not promise an Alberta student that a freeze always exists or works the same way. If a document or device is missing, contact its issuer or service provider promptly. Keep a log of actions, dates, people contacted, and case numbers while storing documents securely.

If money was lost or the person is a victim of fraud, CAFC guidance says to contact local police promptly and report to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre (CAFC). CAFC reports help create a central repository and support investigations; CAFC is not a refund service. Preserve evidence such as receipts, message copies, sender details, dates, account statements, and police file number. Report an unauthorized card transaction to the issuer promptly and follow its instructions. For a data breach, the federal Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) also advises contacting affected businesses, financial institutions, and credit bureaus, and reporting through the National Fraud Reporting System; verify current routes before release.

CRA contact needs precise treatment. CRA can call people; never use the false blanket rule “CRA never calls.” If a contact claims to be CRA and the person is unsure, ask for the caller’s name, office, and callback number, end the call, then verify independently through CRA’s official contact-verification tool or contact details found on Canada.ca. For suspected tax-related identity fraud, contact CRA through an independently verified official route. Do not share passwords or one-time codes with an unexpected contact. A caller knowing personal facts or caller ID showing a government number does not prove authenticity.

Watch for a second wave: a supposed recovery expert may promise guaranteed reimbursement, demand an upfront fee, request remote access, or ask for more identity details. CAFC warns that scammers impersonate authorities and target people who already lost money; CAFC does not contact people to request payment. Stop, preserve the approach as evidence, and verify through the institution or police already contacted. Be kind to the person affected: prompt, practical action matters more than blame. This is a classroom plan, not a substitute for an institution’s current instructions, legal advice, or emergency response. Students complete the task with a fictional case only.
